headline: A New Tool Brings Workspace Hygiene to AI Agents
lede: OpenClaw, the self-hosted AI agent gateway that accumulated roughly 369,000 GitHub stars in its first six months, stores each agent's identity as a directory of plain Markdown files. Those files are powerful but fragile, and until now there was no tooling to tell you when they had gone wrong. A developer known as tolibear_ has built Souls CLI to change that.
body:
OpenClaw is a *self-hosted AI agent gateway* — a single process that runs on a user's own machine and bridges familiar messaging platforms (WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, iMessage) to a large language model capable of browsing the web, managing files, controlling the desktop, and executing multi-step autonomous workflows. Created by Austrian programmer Peter Steinberger and launched in late 2025, it accumulated roughly 369,000 GitHub stars in its first six months — one of the fastest adoption curves in open-source history. Tencent (700.HK) and other companies have announced OpenClaw-based services; a WeChat variant built on DeepSeek appeared in China shortly after launch.

Every OpenClaw agent lives in a *workspace*: a directory of Markdown files at `~/.openclaw/workspace` that, on each session, the gateway reads and assembles into a *system prompt* — the instruction block injected before any user message. The most consequential file is **SOUL.md**, which the official documentation calls the agent's “character sheet”: a structured declaration of values, behavioral guardrails, interaction style, and the meta-instruction that this document is the agent's persistent self-conception across sessions. Without it, the agent is a generic language model with no continuity of identity.

A workspace that begins as a tidy handful of files can degrade quickly. The most costly failure is *token bloat*: a 10,000-character `AGENTS.md` consumes roughly 2,500 *tokens* — the fundamental unit of text an LLM processes, and the unit on which API providers bill — per session before any user message lands. One practitioner documented cutting their monthly API spend from $87 to $27 simply by trimming workspace files. A subtler hazard is silent truncation: when workspace files exceed OpenClaw's internal character limit, the gateway drops content past the cutoff without warning, making rules that appear there invisible to the agent. More insidious is cross-file contradiction — personality notes in SOUL.md that conflict with instructions in AGENTS.md produce unpredictable behavior that is genuinely difficult to diagnose without auditing every file at once. Dynamic strings such as “Current date: May 7, 2026” injected into otherwise static files destroy the *prompt cache*, eliminating the 90 percent token-cost discount that Anthropic provides for stable system prompts.

Souls CLI addresses these failure modes with a terminal interface that discovers every OpenClaw workspace on the machine, grades each one A through F on a percentage scale, and offers a Rescue path for automated repair. The accompanying souls.zip marketplace provides pre-built agent personas and skills, grounded, its makers claim, in over 166 published research papers on agent design. Neither requires a credit card at launch.

tolibear_ is a verified contributor to the official OpenClaw skills repository — having shipped a multi-agent prompt-optimization tool — and received a public acknowledgment from Anthropic's Claude Code team. The product represents a nascent category: *workspace hygiene* automation for personal AI agents. As agent-hosting matures, the gap between a well-tuned and a poorly-tuned workspace translates directly into API costs, behavioral reliability, and the quality of autonomous decisions the agent makes on its owner's behalf.

concepts.definition: Software that bridges a user's preferred messaging apps (WhatsApp, Telegram, etc.) to an AI model capable of taking actions in the world — browsing, file management, calendar control. The gateway handles routing, session state, and tool execution so the AI can operate continuously in the background.

A directory of Markdown files that collectively define an OpenClaw agent's identity, memory, and operating rules. The gateway reads all files on every session and injects their contents into the system prompt before any user message. There is no database — the files are the agent.

The first and most important file in an OpenClaw workspace. Structured into sections covering core values, ethical limits, interaction style, and a meta-instruction acknowledging that the file is the agent's persistent self-conception. Without it, an agent has no stable identity across sessions.

A block of instructions injected by the application before any user message reaches the language model. In OpenClaw, this is assembled from workspace files on every session turn. The system prompt sets the model's persona, capabilities, and behavioral limits.

The accumulation of unnecessary text in an agent's workspace files, causing the system prompt to consume a growing share of tokens on every API call. Because API costs are priced per token, bloated workspaces raise expenses directly and can crowd out useful context.

The fundamental unit of text that large language models process and are billed on. A token is roughly three to four characters of English text. API providers charge per token of input and output, so the size of a system prompt has direct and recurring financial consequences.

An OpenClaw workspace file containing the agent's operating instructions: how it should handle tasks, route requests, manage memory, and interact with tools. When it accumulates conflicting instructions or grows too long, it becomes a primary source of agent misbehavior.

A mechanism offered by some AI providers, including Anthropic, that stores the processed representation of a stable system prompt so it need not be recomputed on every API call. When a system prompt is identical across calls, the provider offers a substantial discount — roughly 90 percent of the input token cost. Any change to the prompt breaks the cache and forfeits the discount.

The practice of keeping an AI agent's workspace files clean, consistent, and token-efficient. Analogous to code linting or database maintenance: the absence of hygiene does not immediately break the system but degrades performance and raises costs over time.

fact_check: The figure of roughly 369,000 GitHub stars would place OpenClaw among the most-starred repositories in GitHub's history for a project of its age; readers should treat this figure as plausible but worth direct verification. The 90 percent prompt-cache discount figure is consistent with Anthropic's published documentation but applies specifically to cache hits on Claude models under their caching pricing tier; other model providers offer different or no caching discounts. The souls.zip claim of grounding in “166+ published research papers” is not independently verifiable from the available sources.
